You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: SpaceX 2026Q2 Earnings Preview: Starlink Operating Margin Rises to 35.9%, AI Compute Contracts Ramp Up Amid Massive August Share Unlock Risks

TEXT:
Core View
SpaceX (SPCX.US) is about to release its second-quarter 2026 earnings. Market attention is focused on the actual contribution pace of its three major businesses (Connectivity/Starlink, AI compute, and Space), as well as the supply pressure from approximately 1.231 billion shares unlocking in August. Existing data imply that full-year revenue requires steep growth in the second half: first-half revenue was about $11.56 billion, while the second half needs to reach approximately $26.6 billion to $34.2 billion. Starlink’s profit margins continue to improve, but whether AI compute leasing contracts can be recognized as revenue on schedule, along with the actual selling behavior of unlocking shareholders, will directly determine the stock’s direction after the results. Current option implied volatility stands at 115%, far higher than the one-month historical volatility of 50%, placing the market in a high-volatility, negative-gamma environment.
Detailed Breakdown
Overall Revenue and Profit Performance
Second-quarter revenue was approximately $6.9 billion, first-quarter revenue about $4.69 billion, and first-half total about $11.56 billion.
Full-year forecasts imply second-half revenue of roughly $26.6 billion to $34.2 billion, meaning a single quarter in the second half may need to grow about 94% to 149% versus the second quarter.
EPS estimates range from a loss of $1.26 per share to a profit of $0.33. UBS expects a diluted loss of $0.12 per share (better than the consensus loss of $0.25), while Morgan Stanley forecasts a loss of $0.35.
Significant divergence exists on profitability, reflecting large differences in institutional assumptions regarding AI and Space business costs and accounting treatments.
Connectivity Business (Starlink) Performance
Second-quarter Connectivity operating margin was approximately 35.9%.
Third-quarter operating margin for this segment is expected to rise further to 37.5%.
Third-quarter Connectivity revenue is projected to grow more than 50% year-over-year to about $4.7 billion.
Steady Starlink expansion remains the foundational business, but user growth alone is insufficient to meet the steep full-year revenue trajectory. Key metrics to watch include net subscriber additions, ARPU, churn rate, and the mix of enterprise and government customers.
Starship’s 13th test flight successfully deployed 20 Starlink V3 satellites, completed in-space engine relight, and achieved a controlled soft splashdown, demonstrating basic capability to deploy V3 satellites and potentially lowering unit capacity costs.
Other Business Segment Performance
AI Business : Currently still loss-making. Signed compute leasing contracts include Anthropic’s access to the Colossus I and Colossus II data centers in Tennessee (standard contract rates once reached $1.25 billion per month) and Alphabet’s arrangement of approximately $920 million per month. Key observation points include contracted and powered-on compute capacity, contract duration, revenue and cost per watt, customer concentration, and the impact of third-party leasing on internal Grok and Cursor training demand. The Anthropic agreement contains flexible termination clauses (either party may cancel with 90 days’ notice after the initial term), while Alphabet’s demand may change as its self-built compute capacity comes online.
Space Business : Starship booster recovery has not yet been completed, and the company remains some distance from a low-cost, high-frequency, airline-like rapid-turnaround model. Management guidance on formal V3 deployment, subsequent test flights, tower catch, and annual launch cadence will be critical.
Capital Expenditure and Long-Term Plans
Overall company capital expenditure is projected to rise from $48.7 billion in 2026 to $118.4 billion in 2028.
Primary investment areas focus on data-center infrastructure, Starlink satellite deployment, and Starship capability upgrades. Whether AI compute contracts can be put into service and recognized as revenue on schedule is the core variable determining whether second-half results can be delivered.
Next-Quarter and Second-Half Guidance Focus Points
The market is primarily waiting for management’s explanation of the second half. The expectation of more than 50% year-over-year growth in third-quarter Connectivity revenue to about $4.7 billion and an operating margin rising to 37.5% must be cross-checked against the actual contribution pace of AI contracts.
Full-year forecasts already embed a steep growth curve; the strength of guidance (especially compute-contract recognition progress and the Starlink V3 deployment timeline) will directly affect post-earnings share-price sustainability.
Market Background and Investor Concerns
Unlock Risk : Approximately 912 million shares become eligible for trading on August 6, with another roughly 319 million shares unlocking about one week later. Current free-float shares stand at about 640 million; the free-float ratio will rise from 4.9% to 11.8%. Potential supply increase already constitutes a clear trading risk.
Options and Technical Picture : Implied volatility is currently 115%, significantly higher than the one-month historical volatility of 50%. The share price sits below the gamma-flip level of $122 in a negative-gamma environment; $100 is a key support level. A break below $100 could trigger a resonance of selling and hedging pressure; a move above $122 would likely reduce the negative-gamma impact.
Core Contradiction : Even if results beat expectations, the share price may not immediately form a one-sided rally. Guidance strength, compute-contract quality (duration, customer concentration, actual power-on and revenue-recognition progress), and the actual selling behavior of unlocking shareholders are the key determinants of whether the post-earnings move can be sustained. The market is effectively betting that large AI compute contracts will begin contributing concentrated revenue.
